findings.summary: decode() closes the OutOfMemoryError route with its stream/pod count bounds, and leaves five easier routes to an UNCHECKED exception out of the same `throws IOException` method wide open: every value it reads off the wire is fed straight into a validating record. MEASURED against the staged bytes, each of these decodes to an IllegalArgumentException rather than an IOException -- (a) oldestRetainedOffset > nextOffset -> 'oldestRetainedOffset 6 is past nextOffset 5' (line 384, StreamOffsets); (b) a zero-length podId -> 'a podId is never blank' (line 394, compact constructor); (c) a partitionId uvarint of 0x80000000 truncating to negative -> 'partitionId is never negative: -2147483648' (line 381-382, RunKey); (d) a full-width varint sequence -> 'sequence is never negative: -1' (line 366); (e) a full-width varint flushSeq -> 'lastAppliedFlushSeq is never negative: poda' (line 395). The same package already states and solves this exactly: ChainEntry.decodeKinded wraps its record construction in `catch (IllegalArgumentException e) -> new IOException(...)` under the comment 'a value the WIRE can carry but a record refuses is corrupt input, not a programming error ... Unwrapped, a torn or zero-filled object would throw an unchecked exception straight past recover's own throws IOException and every caller catching it.' Checkpoint carries MORE such invariants than any chain entry (the cross-field oldest<=next check has no analogue in a delta), so it is the most exposed decoder in the module and the only one that does not wrap. The diff's own test bytesThatAreNotACheckpointAreRefusedRatherThanMisread shows the intended contract -- malformed bytes are refused as IOException -- and only exercises the two routes that happen to work (bad magic, short header).
findings.failure_scenario: M4.9 reads the newest checkpoint and, following CommitLog.recover and ChainReplay.read, catches IOException to treat a torn or foreign object as corrupt. A checkpoint truncated mid-write, or one whose bytes were reordered, decodes into oldest>next or a zero-length podId and throws IllegalArgumentException straight through that catch: takeover dies with an unchecked exception on the recovery path, with a message about a record invariant rather than about a corrupt object, and no caller can distinguish it from a programming error. Because this is the commit that fixes the format's reader contract, the wrong contract is what M4.9 will be written against.

findings.summary: Both decode loops put into a LinkedHashMap, so a repeated RunKey or podId on the wire silently LAST-WINS instead of being refused, and the trailing-bytes check at line 397 still passes. Measured: bytes claiming two entries for the same RunKey, first nextOffset=900 then nextOffset=5, decode to a one-entry checkpoint at nextOffset=5 -- an offset that went BACKWARDS. CommitDelta's compact constructor refuses the identical shape for segment keys and states why in as many words ('a delta with duplicate keys arriving from a torn object or a foreign writer would decode without complaint'), i.e. the project already treats this as rung 1 rather than as a caller's problem. Separately and in the same constructor, the pods map is validated entry by entry (null value, blank key, negative seq) while the streams map is validated not at all -- `new LinkedHashMap<>(streams)` accepts a null key or a null StreamOffsets that Map.copyOf would have rejected.
findings.failure_scenario: A checkpoint whose bytes were torn or written by a foreign build carries a stream twice; recovery adopts the later, lower nextOffset, and the sequencer reassigns offsets it has already handed out -- silent duplication, which is what invariant I2 forbids, and the loud-failure property ADR-0033 claims for a misread checkpoint does not apply because these bytes carry the right magic. For the second half: a caller building the streams map with a null value constructs a Checkpoint successfully and NPEs later inside encode(), on the leader's write path, rather than at construction where the pods map would have refused.

findings.summary: `c.bytes((int) c.uvarint())` narrows a 64-bit wire length to int with no cap and no check that the cast was lossless. A length of 0x1_0000_0004 truncates to 4 and the object decodes as valid rather than being refused -- measured, decoding to pods={aaaa=7}. Cursor.bytes then bounds the allocation, so this is not an OOM route, but it is a silent misread. This is the same expression as CommitDelta.readSegment:238, and backlog row M0.55 already names its other half ('cap the segment-key length') as an open wire-format-change checklist item; the new decoder inherits the gap rather than closing it.
findings.failure_scenario: A torn checkpoint whose podId length field is corrupted in the high bits decodes into a checkpoint carrying a podId that no pod has, with a lastAppliedFlushSeq attached to it. Recovery adopts the bogus entry, the real pod's entry is missing, and its next retried flush is not recognised as a replay -- the exact silent duplication the podId->lastAppliedFlushSeq map exists to prevent.

notes: Verified independently, in an isolated copy of the staged bytes, by mutation and by probe (both probe files deleted afterwards; the repository was not touched). WHAT HOLDS: (1) COST -- nothing in this diff issues an object-store request; the format module is pure encode/decode and no caller is added. The shape does not commit the project to a forbidden rate either: one checkpoint is ONE object carrying every stream and every pod, so a future writer's PUT rate is per checkpoint (M4.8b's K deltas or T seconds), never per stream, index, partition or record. Checkpoint SIZE grows with streams, which is bytes and not requests, and it is what keeps the object count flat. No idle-path request is added. (2) THE SIZE CLAIM IS REAL AND THE MAGNITUDE IS RIGHT -- measured the 1,600-stream fixture at 36,690 bytes (35.8 KiB), inside the test's 20..64 KiB bracket and matching both the row's '~38 KiB' and research 03-metadata-and-cas.md section 9's '1,600 streams x ~24 B ~= 38 KiB' (23 B/stream here, since the 16-byte UUID is paid in full). A fleet-sized variant at 200 pods is 39,775 bytes, still inside the bracket. (3) THE GOLDEN FILE IS HAND-VERIFIABLE AND I VERIFIED IT BYTE BY BYTE: 148 bytes total (the figure ADR-0033 quotes), '42 43 4b 50' = BCKP, '00 00 00 00' = version 0, '09' = sequence, '06' = six streams, 'e9 07' = 1001 and '64' = 100 for stream 1, 'f6 2e' = 6006 and 'd8 04' = 600 for stream 6, tail '02 04 poda 2a 04 podb 4d' = two pods at 42 and 77. The streams appear in ASCENDING key order in the file while the fixture inserts them descending, so the sort really is pinned by the bytes. (4) THE COUNT BOUNDS ARE SAFE, including the two I was asked to check: the smallest stream is 19 bytes (16 + three 1-byte uvarints) and the divisor is 18, and the smallest pod is 2 bytes against a divisor of 1 -- both LOOSER than the layout allows, but loose in the safe direction, and neither count sizes any collection (both maps are default-capacity and filled in the loop, unlike CommitDelta's `new ArrayList<>((int) count)`), so the guard is a fail-fast in front of a loop that would fail on its first short read anyway. Measured: 0x7FFFFFFF streams is refused as IOException. (5) ORDERING AND EQUALITY ARE CONSISTENT -- RunKey.compareTo is a total order consistent with equals (UUID then partitionId), String.compareTo is total and not locale-sensitive, keys come from a keySet so there are no ties, and encode() canonicalises; therefore two Checkpoints that Map.equals considers equal always encode to identical bytes, and the order-insensitivity of the record's generated equals/hashCode cannot contradict the encoder. Preserving the caller's order in the value type is the right trade here: it is the only deterministic way to pin a deleted sort, it is documented on the constructor, and it is invisible to equals. (6) ADR-0033's factual claims check out against the tree: ChainReplay.applyChain does LIST plus one GET per key and chainEnd takes the last key under logPrefix as the chain end (the ADR's compound sentence merges the two methods, which is the phrasing M4.8b's row already uses); BCKP = 0x42434B50 is distinct from BDLT = 0x42444C54, so a checkpoint read by ChainEntry.decode fails with 'not a chain entry: bad magic' and a delta read by Checkpoint.decode fails likewise -- I confirmed both directions; and research 03-metadata-and-cas.md section 9 is UNCHANGED by this decision, so the wire-format-change checklist's 'update the research document with a banner if a conclusion changed' does not fire. (7) SCOPE -- no writer, no trigger, no key grammar, nothing outside format/ and docs/; the backlog row moves to backlog-done.md and its notes section stays, which matches how M4.17 and other landed rows are kept. WHAT I DID NOT CHECK: compilation, test pass/fail, formatting, file size and links, all owned by the gates listed in the packet.
